motivating_questions.content: To theoretically scrutinize the electronic properties of α-(BETS)₂I₃—a molecular Dirac system with strong SOC—a low-energy Hamiltonian that faithfully reflects the full ab initio band structure is indispensable. Earlier attempts to extract tight-binding parameters for this material faced the challenge that many transfer integrals contribute in a narrow energy window around the Dirac points, and efficient methods for incorporating SOC into effective models had not been established for such complex molecular solids. Without a reliable tight-binding model, the calculation of transport coefficients, the role of the imaginary transfer energies, and quantitative comparisons with experiment remained out of reach.

conclusion.content:
A momentum-space three-orbital tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating a Kane–Mele type spin–orbit coupling (SOC) is derived from first-principles Wannier fitting for both [Pt(dmdt)2] and [Ni(dmdt)2]. The kinetic plus SOC Hamiltonian is
      $$
      H=\sum_{\langle i,\alpha:j,\beta\rangle,s} t_{i,\alpha;j,\beta}\,c^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,s}c_{j,\beta,s}
      + i\lambda\sum_{\langle i,\alpha:j,\beta\rangle,s} \nu_{i,\alpha;j,\beta}\, t_{i,\alpha;j,\beta}\, c^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha,s}\,\sigma^z_{ss}\,c_{j,\beta,s},
      $$
      where $c_{i,\alpha,s}^{(\dagger)}$ annihilates (creates) an electron of spin $s\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}$ on Wannier fragment orbital $\alpha\in\{A,B,C\}$ in unit cell $i$, $t_{i\alpha;j\beta}$ are the Wannier hoppings obtained by fitting, $\lambda$ is the SOC strength, and $\nu_{i\alpha;j\beta}\in\{0,\pm1\}$ encodes the bond-dependent sign of the SOC term. In $\mathbf{k}$-space the matrix elements $H_{\alpha\beta,s}(\mathbf{k})$ (for $\alpha,\beta=A,B,C$ and spin $s$) are:
      \begin{align*}
      H_{AA,s}(\mathbf{k}) &= -2t_9\cos k_a,\\
      H_{AB,s}(\mathbf{k}) &= t_{13}e^{i(-k_a+k_b+k_c)} - t_1 + t_5(1+i\lambda\sigma)e^{i(k_b+k_c)} + t_4(1-i\lambda\sigma)e^{ik_c},\\
      H_{AC,s}(\mathbf{k}) &= -t_{11}e^{i(-k_a+k_b+k_c)} - t_{12}e^{i(k_a+k_c)} - t_6 - t_3e^{ik_c} - t_2e^{i(k_b+k_c)},\\
      H_{BB,s}(\mathbf{k}) &= \Delta + 2t_7\cos(k_b+k_c) - 2t_8\cos k_c - 2t_{10}\cos k_a,\\
      H_{BC,s}(\mathbf{k}) &= t_{13}e^{i(-k_a+k_b+k_c)} - t_1 + t_5(1-i\lambda\sigma)e^{i(k_b+k_c)} + t_4(1+i\lambda\sigma)e^{ik_c},\\
      H_{CC,s}(\mathbf{k}) &= -2t_9\cos k_a,

Wannier orbitals were extracted from the first-principles Kohn-Sham states using the Wannier90 software, producing a localized basis spanning the $p_z$ manifold: Wannier orbitals for C-$p_z$ and B-$p_z$ were extracted for monolayer and alkali-intercalated $BC_3$, and C-$p_z$ orbitals were extracted for graphene; the Wannierization used the indicated $\boldsymbol{k}$-meshes described in the computational protocol.

The tight-binding interpolation Hamiltonian was defined as $\hat{\mathcal{H}} = \sum_{i,j} t_{i,j} \hat{c}_i^\dagger \hat{c}_j$, where $t_{i,j}$ denotes the transfer integral between Wannier orbitals indexed by $i$ and $j$, and $\hat{c}_i^\dagger$ ($\hat{c}_j$) denote the electron creation (annihilation) operators for the Wannier state $i$ ($j$); this Hamiltonian is used purely as an interpolation device to reproduce first-principles dispersions and their derivatives on dense $\boldsymbol{k}$-meshes for transport evaluation.

Validation: comparison of the tight-binding band dispersions (Wannier interpolation) with the first-principles band dispersions shows close agreement on the energy windows of interest, demonstrating that the Wannier-derived tight-binding Hamiltonian reproduces the first-principles bands with high fidelity and therefore can be used to evaluate energies and group velocities on very fine $\boldsymbol{k}$-meshes; this agreement is visualized by the overlapping first-principles (blue solid) and tight-binding (red dotted) bands. 
Fig. 2(a)

Using the Wannier-derived tight-binding Hamiltonian, band energies $E_{n,\boldsymbol{k}}$ and group velocities $\boldsymbol{v}_{n,\boldsymbol{k}} = \frac{1}{\hbar}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{k}} E_{n,\boldsymbol{k}}$ were computed on very fine $\boldsymbol{k}$-meshes; these quantities are the system-dependent inputs required for Boltzmann transport integrals (transport coefficient tensors $K_i$) under the relaxation-time approximation, enabling high-resolution mapping of conduction-band energy on the $(k_x,k_y)$ plane and accurate numerical evaluation of transport tensors. 
Fig. 2(c)

Because the transport tensors $K_i$ require only band energies and group velocities (and an assumed relaxation time), the tight-binding interpolation yields transport coefficients equivalent to first-principles results insofar as the tight-binding dispersion reproduces the first-principles dispersion; this justifies using the Wannier-derived tight-binding Hamiltonian to obtain dense-mesh transport integrals for $BC_3$.

Define the four-orbital $\pi$-band tight-binding Hamiltonian $H(\mathbf{k})$ as the $\mathbf{k}$-dependent $4\times4$ matrix with a $2\times2$ bottom-layer block $H_B(\mathbf{k})$, a $2\times2$ top-layer block $H_T(\mathbf{k})$, and off-diagonal interlayer blocks $H_{BT}(\mathbf{k})$ and $H_{TB}(\mathbf{k})$, written in block form as
$$
H(\mathbf{k})=\begin{pmatrix}
H_B(\mathbf{k}) & H_{BT}(\mathbf{k}) \\
H_{TB}(\mathbf{k}) & H_T(\mathbf{k})
\end{pmatrix},
$$
where $\mathbf{k}$ is the crystal momentum in the two-dimensional Brillouin zone. This block form is the starting structural definition of the model. Fig. 2

Express each Hamiltonian matrix element $H_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k})$ (where indices $\alpha,\beta\in\{A,B,A',B'\}$ label sublattices: $A,B$ bottom layer, $A',B'$ top layer) as a sum over symmetry-grouped structure-factor terms of two types: intersublattice structure factors $f_n(\mathbf{k})$ and intrasublattice structure factors $g_n(\mathbf{k})$, according to
$$
H_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_n t_{\alpha\beta n}\, f_n(\mathbf{k})\quad\text{or}\quad H_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_n t'_{\alpha\beta n}\, g_n(\mathbf{k}),
$$
where $t_{\alpha\beta n}$ and $t'_{\alpha\beta n}$ are hopping coefficients (in eV) associated with group $n$, and $f_n(\mathbf{k})$ and $g_n(\mathbf{k})$ are structure-factor functions defined by lattice symmetry (explicit forms for $f_n(\mathbf{k})$ and $g_n(\mathbf{k})$ up to $n=2$ are given in the paper's definitions and Appendix A). This is the formal decomposition that organizes microscopic hoppings into symmetry-equivalent groups. Appendix A

State the electronic-structure calculation framework used to obtain the hopping coefficients: perform local-density-approximation (LDA) first-principles calculations (Perdew-Zunger parametrization of the LDA) to obtain Bloch bands and then construct maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) centered on carbon $p_z$ orbitals using the plane-wave code QUANTUM ESPRESSO and WANNIER90. Here LDA denotes the local-density approximation, MLWF denotes maximally localized Wannier functions, QUANTUM ESPRESSO is the plane-wave first-principles package, and WANNIER90 is the MLWF construction package. The computed MLWFs are orthonormal localized orbitals centered at the carbon sites and define the tight-binding hopping matrix elements by matrix elements of the Hamiltonian between Wannier orbitals. [17]
[18]
[19]
[20]

Relate the Wannier representation hopping amplitudes $t_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}')$ to the Bloch Hamiltonian matrix elements via
$$
H_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{R},\mathbf{R}'} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{R}'-\mathbf{R})}\, t_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}'),
$$
where $t_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}')=\langle\mathbf{R}+\tau_\alpha|H|\mathbf{R}'+\tau_\beta'\rangle$ is the hopping from Wannier orbital at site $\beta$ (position $\mathbf{R}'+\tau_\beta'$) to site $\alpha$ (position $\mathbf{R}+\tau_\alpha$), $N$ is the number of unit cells, and $\tau_\alpha$ denotes the sublattice position vector. This relation defines how the MLWF matrix elements map to $H(\mathbf{k})$. Appendix A

Describe computational details and numerical sampling that determine model completeness: use a $30\times30$ $\mathbf{k}$-point sampling density in the Brillouin zone for the LDA and MLWF construction, which yields converged hopping parameters up to hopping groups indexed through $n\leq17$ (i.e., up to 17 in-plane distant neighbor groups); the paper reports that the $30\times30$ Wannier interpolation reproduces LDA $\pi$-band energies throughout the Brillouin zone to numerical accuracy set by this dense sampling, whereas coarser sampling (e.g., $6\times6$) produces visible deviations near the $M$ point of up to $\sim0.2$ eV. This establishes the claimed numerical accuracy of the constructed model. Fig. 2

Report that the full tight-binding (FTB) model constructed from the MLWF matrix elements therefore includes hopping amplitudes associated with symmetry-grouped structure factors up to 17 distinct in-plane neighbor groups, with numerical hopping amplitudes listed explicitly in Appendix B Tables IV and V (values given in eV for each $n$ and for each matrix-element family, including multiplicities and in-plane projected distances). These tabulated hopping amplitudes are the microscopic, site-centered, orthonormal-orbital matrix elements that constitute the FTB model. Appendix B Tables IV and V

Assert that the MLWF-based FTB model reproduces the LDA $\pi$-band energies across the entire Brillouin zone: the Wannier-interpolated band structure computed from the FTB Hamiltonian with the listed hopping amplitudes matches the LDA bands for the $30\times30$ sampling and therefore reproduces band energies to the numerical accuracy limited by that sampling; this is supported by the close agreement shown between Wannier-interpolated bands and first-principles LDA bands in the interpolation comparison and by the statement that hoppings more remote than those listed are negligible for the $30\times30$ sampling. Fig. 2

Conclude that because the Wannier functions are orthonormal and site-centered on carbon $p_z$ orbitals, the FTB model's hopping matrix elements admit the microscopic physical interpretation of tunneling matrix elements between $p_z$-derived Wannier orbitals; therefore the model provides physically interpretable microscopic hopping parameters and an ab initio four-orbital $\pi$-band tight-binding Hamiltonian that reproduces LDA bands. This links the mathematical Hamiltonian construction to physical orbital-based interpretation. [12]

motivating_questions.content: In bilayer graphene modeling, there was no direct, orbital-resolved tight-binding Hamiltonian derived from first principles that both (i) uses an orthonormal localized basis so that hopping matrix elements can be unambiguously interpreted as intersite tunneling between $p_z$-like orbitals, and (ii) reproduces LDA band energies across the full Brillouin zone. Prior tight-binding parameter sets were typically obtained by fits or by analogy with graphite (SWM), which left significant ambiguity about which microscopic hopping processes (their magnitudes, ranges, and signs) are important. Without a faithful ab initio model, predictions for global band features (away from Dirac points) and for wave-function character could not be made with controlled confidence, obstructing reliable derivations of effective low-energy models and comparisons to many-body or experimental data.

motivating_questions.content: Accurate transport calculations for a long metal–semiconductor–metal lateral heterojunction require a finite-dimensional tight-binding representation that (i) captures the multi-orbital character (transition-metal $d$ and chalcogen $p$ orbitals), (ii) preserves spin–orbit coupling and valley structure, and (iii) allows connecting semi-infinite pristine leads to a finite scattering region. motivating_questions.content: In studying superconductivity one needs a minimal electronic model that accurately describes electronic states near the Fermi level so that pairing interactions can be evaluated and self-consistent superconducting solutions can be computed. Prior tight-binding parameterizations for MoS₂ employed different orbital sets and parameter choices; without a fit specifically focused on the conduction-band minimum it is unclear which minimal orbital content and hopping parameters reliably describe the low-energy carriers introduced by electron doping. Without such a validated low-energy model, subsequent calculations of pairing interactions, screening, and $T_c(n)$ lack a firm band-structure foundation. The three-orbital conduction-band parametrization addresses the need for a compact, accurate electronic model (explicit orbital content, on-site energies, and hopping integrals) that is suitable for constructing a BCS pairing problem for electron-doped monolayer MoS₂.

A local environment tight-binding Hamiltonian of the form
$$
H_{\mathrm{LETB}}=\sum_{ij\sigma} t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}\big(\vec{R}_i,\vec{R}_j,\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}\big)\,c_{i\sigma}^\dagger c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.},
$$
where $t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}$ depends on the pair positions and the local set of nearby nuclear coordinates $\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}$, was constructed by combining the intralayer regression models (conclusion 1) and the refitted FK interlayer form (conclusion 2), and trained on a dataset of 72 distinct deformed bilayer graphene primitive-cell configurations. premises.content: The DFT calculations (using the BEEF-VDW van der Waals functional and a polarized triple-$\zeta$ all-electron basis) that produce the training data are validated against angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) for AB bilayer graphene (Fig. 12).  Near the Fermi level, the DFT and ARPES dispersions agree within $0.1$ eV, and the deviation increases away from the $K$ point but does not exceed $10\%$ of the experimental binding energy.
premises.metadata: {"role": "highlight", "conclusion_id": "3", "strength_types": ["measurement", "external"], "credit": "This external validation against experimental data shows that the DFT functional (BEEF-VDW) provides a faithful description of the $\\pi$ bands in bilayer graphene, the same electronic manifold that the LETB aims to model.  Because the LETB is trained on DFT-derived Wannier hoppings, any systematic error in DFT would be inherited by the LETB.  The ARPES comparison partially bounds these errors to the $\\sim 0.1$ eV level for low-energy bands, which is about $10$\u2013$20\\%$ of typical nearest-neighbor hopping magnitudes but much larger than the meV-scale bandwidth at the magic angle.  However, the comparison shows that DFT is quantitatively reliable for the band structure that the LETB reproduces, supporting the credibility of the LETB training data and thus the physical relevance of the LETB predictions.  Without this external check, one could argue that the LETB faithfully reproduces only the DFT (which itself might be inaccurate), but the ARPES agreement shows that the DFT is a reasonable target."}

The intralayer tight-binding hopping terms for first-, second-, and third-nearest neighbors are quantitatively described by linear regression models that include explicit local-environment geometric descriptors, with the following fitted forms (cross-validated parameter means and standard deviations over five folds):
      - nearest-neighbor (1-NN) intralayer hopping: $t_{1} = -9.68(4) + 2.52(1)\,a$,
      - second-nearest-neighbor (2-NN) intralayer hopping: $t_{2} = 1.55(1) + 0.022(2)\,b -0.66(1)\,h_1 -0.20(1)\,h_2$,
      - third-nearest-neighbor (3-NN) intralayer hopping: $t_{3} = -1.23(1) + 0.04(1)\,c -0.12(1)\,h + 0.23(1)\,l$.
      Here $a$, $b$, $c$ are the interatomic distances for first-, second-, and third-nearest-neighbor pairs, respectively; $h_1$ and $h_2$ are local-hexagon-shape descriptors that parametrize the shape of the hexagon formed by the six atoms surrounding the hopping centers; and $h$ and $l$ are hexagon-size descriptors that parametrize the size of the entire hexagonal environment around the hopping centers. These models were selected by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) feature selection and fitted by five-fold cross-validated ordinary least-squares regression, and they achieve high predictive quality ($R^2$ values of 0.98 for 1-NN and 0.96 for 3-NN), demonstrating that distance-only parametrizations fail (especially for 2-NN and 3-NN) and that explicit many-atom geometric descriptors are required for quantitatively accurate intralayer hoppings.

premises.content:
The interlayer hopping is parametrized using the Fang–Kaxiras functional form
      $$
      t^{\mathrm{FK}}(\vec{r},\theta_u,\theta_d)=V_0(r_{xy}/a)+V_3(r_{xy}/a)\big[\cos(3\theta_u)+\cos(3\theta_d)\big]+V_6(r_{xy}/a)\big[\cos(6\theta_u)+\cos(6\theta_d)\big],
      $$
      with
      $V_0(r)=\lambda_0 e^{-\xi_0 r^2}\cos(\kappa_0 r),\quad
      V_3(r)=\lambda_3 r^2 e^{-\xi_3(r-x_3)^2},\quad
      V_6(r)=\lambda_6 e^{-\xi_6(r-x_6)^2}\sin(\kappa_6 r).$
      Here $r_{xy}$ is the pair distance projected onto the $x$-$y$ plane, $\theta_u$ indicates the orientation of the nearest-neighbor triangle of the upper sheet atom relative to the displacement vector, $\theta_d$ is the corresponding angle for the lower sheet atom, $a = a_0/\sqrt{3} = 1.549$ bohr. The nonlinear least-squares refit to the DFT/Wannier dataset yields cross-validated parameter means with standard deviations over five folds: $\lambda_0=239(2)\,\mathrm{meV}$, $\xi_0=2.12(2)$, $\kappa_0=1.871(4)$; $\lambda_3=-40(1)\,\mathrm{meV}$, $\xi_3=3.8(4)$, $x_3=0.52(4)$; $\lambda_6=-5.9(7)\,\mathrm{meV}$, $\xi_6=6.0(8)$, $x_6=1.52(1)$, $\kappa_6=1.73(2)$. The refitted FK model captures DFT interlayer hoppings across short, intermediate, and long projected pair distances and corrects the intermediate-distance ($\sim$7–10 bohr) deficiencies of simpler distance-only parametrizations.

Specify the LETB Hamiltonian functional form and symbol definitions used to assemble the model: define
$
H_{\mathrm{LETB}}=\sum_{ij\sigma} t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}\big(\vec{R}_i,\vec{R}_j,\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}\big)\,c_{i\sigma}^\dagger c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.},

where $i,j$ label atomic sites, $\sigma$ is spin, $c_{i\sigma}^\dagger$ creates a localized $p_z$-character orbital on site $i$ with spin $\sigma$, $\vec{R}_i$ is the position of atom $i$, and $\{\vec{R}_{ij}\}$ denotes the set of nearby nuclear coordinates that define the local environment used to evaluate the environment-dependent hopping function $t_{ij}^{\mathrm{LETB}}$. This is the general LETB Ansatz used in the paper.

Describe the classification and computation pipeline that maps a given atomic configuration to a set of hoppings: (a) for each pair $i,j$ compute the displacement vector $\vec{d}=\vec{R}_i-\vec{R}_j$, (b) classify the hopping as intralayer if $|d_z|<1\,$bohr and as interlayer otherwise, (c) if intralayer, classify neighbor order via the in-plane distance $d_{xy}=\sqrt{d_x^2+d_y^2}$ into 1-NN, 2-NN, or 3-NN if $d_{xy}$ is within $\pm5\%$ of equilibrium distances $a_0$, $\sqrt{3}a_0$, and $2a_0$ respectively, (d) for in-bound classifications (interlayer and intralayer up to 3-NN) collect all atoms within $2a_0$ of atoms $i$ and $j$ to compute the required local-environment descriptors (the $h_1,h_2,h,l$ etc.), and (e) evaluate the hopping using the fitted intralayer linear regression models for 1/2/3-NN or the refitted FK interlayer formula as appropriate; return zero for out-of-bounds intralayer hoppings.

motivating_questions.content: To test whether conclusions about band flattening, band isolation, and fragile topology are robust, a compact, transferable TB model is required that (i) is faithful to ab initio Wannierized parameters across representative local geometries and (ii) can be affordably evaluated across many twisted unit cells and relaxation states. Direct DFT on large moiré cells is too expensive for broad parameter sweeps, and phenomenological TB models lack first-principles calibration. The LETB Hamiltonian provides a middle ground: an explicit local-environment-dependent TB form whose parameters are directly regressed from a DFT/Wannier dataset, enabling many-band calculations that preserve DFT accuracy at greatly reduced cost.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A full-range ab-initio tight-binding Hamiltonian (FTBH) for monolayer TMDCs has been constructed by performing a unitary Wannier transformation of Kohn–Sham DFT bands using as projections the metal $d$ orbitals and the chalcogen $p$ orbitals and retaining the four lowest conduction and seven highest valence bands. The real-space FTBH is an eleven-orbital per unit-cell Hamiltonian whose matrix elements are the ab-initio Wannier matrix elements (hoppings and on-site energies) and which reproduces the DFT (and, where computed, GW) bandstructure to within a few meV on a $25\times25\times1$ $k$-grid. (1)), and the Wannier functions are localized and close to atomic orbitals so that the FTBH provides an ab-initio, orthonormal basis preserving orbital phases and crystal symmetries.

steps.reasoning:
State the computational starting point and methods used to construct an ab-initio lattice Hamiltonian: Kohn–Sham density-functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed with plane-wave basis and projector-augmented wave pseudopotentials using the VASP implementation, with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof generalized-gradient approximation for exchange-correlation; the calculations used a slab geometry with a 20 Å vacuum region, geometry relaxation until Hellmann–Feynman forces < 0.01 eV/Å, a plane-wave cutoff of 450 eV, and a $25\times25\times1$ reciprocal-space sampling grid. 
[29,30]

Define the objective of producing a full-range tight-binding Hamiltonian: construct a real-space, orthonormal, ab-initio-derived Hamiltonian in a localized Wannier basis that (i) retains all orbitals relevant near the Fermi level (metal $d$ and chalcogen $p$), (ii) preserves orbital phases and crystal symmetries, and (iii) reproduces DFT (and where available GW) quasiparticle bands with high numerical accuracy on the chosen $k$-grid.

Introduce the Wannier transformation used to obtain the full-range tight-binding Hamiltonian (FTBH): perform a unitary transformation from Bloch eigenstates to maximally-localized Wannier functions (MLWF) using the Wannier90 implementation, with initial projections chosen to be atomic metal $d$ orbitals and chalcogen $p$ orbitals; the final Wannier functions converge to functions that are localized and close to atomic orbitals and form an orthonormal basis for the lattice Hamiltonian. 
[32]

Specify the orbital subspace retained in the Wannierization and thereby the size of the FTBH Hilbert space: retain the four lowest conduction bands and the seven highest valence bands, whose dominant orbital characters are metal $d$ and chalcogen $p$ orbitals, resulting in an eleven-orbital per primitive-cell Wannier basis with the ordered orbital list 
$[\,d_{z^{2}},\,d_{xy},\,d_{x^{2}-y^{2}},\,d_{xz},\,d_{yz},\,p_{x}^{A},\,p_{y}^{A},\,p_{z}^{A},\,p_{x}^{B},\,p_{y}^{B},\,p_{z}^{B}\,]$,
as used in the construction. 
(Here $p^{A}$/$p^{B}$ label the top/bottom chalcogen atoms in the monolayer unit cell.)

Define the FTBH as the matrix of ab-initio Wannier matrix elements: denote the Wannier-orbital creation operators collectively and write the full-range tight-binding Hamiltonian as a real-space Hamiltonian whose on-site energies and hopping matrix elements are the ab-initio Wannier matrix elements extracted from the DFT Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian after the unitary Wannier transformation; these matrix elements are interpreted as the exact ab-initio hopping and on-site terms in the localized Wannier basis and form the entries of the eleven-orbital per-cell real-space Hamiltonian.

Report the numerical accuracy of the FTBH compared to the originating ab-initio bands on the employed sampling: with the Wannier construction sampled on a $25\times25\times1$ $k$-point grid, the FTBH reproduces the DFT bandstructure (and, where computed, GW quasiparticle bands) to within a few meV across the sampled Brillouin zone, i.e., the numerical discrepancy between FTBH eigenvalues and DFT/GW eigenvalues is on the order of a few meV for this sampling.

Assert the locality and atomic-like character of the Wannier functions and the preservation of orbital phases and crystal symmetries: the converged Wannier functions are localized and close to atomic $d$ and $p$ orbitals (as a result of the atomic-orbital initial projections), so the FTBH provides an orthonormal, symmetry-respecting orbital basis that preserves relative orbital phases, enabling correct computation of quantities sensitive to orbital phases (for example optical matrix elements and Berry curvature) and providing a controlled ab-initio starting point for many-body Hamiltonians.

motivating_questions.content: In studies that require both quantitative accuracy and orbital-phase information (for example, calculation of optical matrix elements, Berry curvature, and construction of many-body Hamiltonians), it is insufficient to use either overly simplified few-orbital models that omit important chalcogen $p$ contributions, or fitted multi-parameter tight-binding models that sacrifice orbital-phase fidelity and orthogonality. A compact, ab-initio-derived Hamiltonian in a minimal but complete orbital set was needed to provide a consistent starting point for both single-layer and multilayer TMDC electronic structure and downstream many-body and optical calculations; prior work did not supply such a Wannier-derived eleven-band Hamiltonian that simultaneously preserves symmetry, orbital character, and orthogonality with ab-initio accuracy.

$$

premises.content: The study identifies and validates a minimal orbital basis sufficient to capture the bands near the Fermi level in both $\alpha\alpha$ and $\alpha\beta$ systems: (i) graphene-derived $\pi$ orbitals with dominant C-$p_z$ character to represent valence-band edge states ($b_v$), and (ii) fluorographene antibonding $\mathcal{A}$ orbitals (primarily C-$p_z$ and F-$p_z$ mixed character, centered on C–F pairs) that hybridize with $\pi$ states to form the conduction-band edge ($b_c$). Using these choices as initial projections, maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) were computed with WANNIER90 that closely resemble the proposed atomic-like $\pi$ and $\mathcal{A}$ orbitals and reproduce the DFT Kohn–Sham character in the selected energy window. This defines a compact 24-orbital per unit-cell basis (e.g., 12 $\pi$ + 12 $\mathcal{A}$ for the 6-$\alpha\alpha$ case) adequate to represent the low-energy manifold.

steps.reasoning: Starting point (upstream result assumed known): the MLWF basis $\{\pi,\mathcal{A}\}$ and the spin-unpolarized/polarized DFT Kohn–Sham states contained in the selected energy window have been established and validated (conclusion: minimal Wannier basis and MLWFs reproducing DFT character are available). These MLWFs provide the localized orbital set used to construct a tight-binding Hamiltonian.

Construction of the spin-resolved Wannier tight-binding Hamiltonian: using the computed maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) in the $\{\pi,\mathcal{A}\}$ basis, a spin-resolved tight-binding Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ with spin index $\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow$ is generated by projecting the DFT Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian onto the MLWF basis and Fourier transforming to obtain hopping and on-site matrix elements that can depend on spin in spin-polarized calculations; the spin-resolved $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ therefore encodes site energies $\varepsilon_{j\sigma}$ and hopping matrix elements $t_{jl}$ that reflect the DFT spin polarization.

Exact reproduction of DFT eigenvalues/eigenvectors within the Wannier window: by construction, the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ reproduce the DFT Kohn–Sham eigenvalues and eigenvectors exactly within the chosen energy window used for Wannierization, because WANNIER90 produces an exact unitary transformation between the selected Bloch subspace and the MLWF subspace. Consequently, $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ provides an exact single-particle mapping from DFT to a localized tight-binding representation for the targeted low-energy bands.

Empirical validation against DFT band structures: comparison plots of DFT spin-polarized bands (points) and the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ (lines) for $n$-$\alpha\alpha$ and $n$-$\alpha\beta$ systems demonstrate excellent agreement near the Fermi level for the bands derived from the $\pi$ and $\mathcal{A}$ orbitals; for the $\alpha\beta$ systems the majority/minority spin bands from $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ match the spin-split DFT bands, and for $\alpha\alpha$ the spin-degenerate bands coincide. This empirical agreement is presented and quantified by direct band-structure overlays.

Concluding statement linking the Wannier Hamiltonian to DFT fidelity: because $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ is constructed from the MLWFs that reproduce the DFT Bloch subspace within the chosen energy window, and because the $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ eigenvalues and eigenvectors match the DFT spin-polarized band structures for both $n$-$\alpha\alpha$ and $n$-$\alpha\beta$ systems (as evidenced by the overlays), $\mathcal{H}_W^\sigma$ provides an exact mapping (within the Wannier energy window) from DFT to a localized spin-resolved tight-binding representation suitable for model reduction and interacting-model parameter extraction.

motivating_questions.content: A prerequisite for building an interacting Anderson–Hubbard model is an exact single-particle representation of the DFT results in a localized basis so that hopping matrix elements and spin-dependent on-site energies can be unambiguously extracted. Prior work did not supply an explicit, spin-resolved Wannier Hamiltonian for these graphene/fluorographene superlattices. Without such a Hamiltonian, derivation of interaction parameters and systematic simplification to reduced-neighbor models would lack a rigorous ab initio foundation, preventing faithful reproduction of DFT magnetism and spectral features in reduced models.
